outline.description: This opening chapter situates Jimenez v. Bondi within the Tenth Circuit’s asylum jurisprudence, outlines the parties’ relief sought, the procedural posture leading to the appellate review, and clarifies the scope of the court’s jurisdiction under 8 U.S.C. §1252.
subtopics: Case citation, docket number, and deciding judge
Relief sought: affirmative asylum and withholding of removal (CAT claim excluded from appeal)
The immigration judge’s denial and BIA affirmation
Petitioners’ petition for review under §1252(a)(1)–(b)(9)
Limits on appellate review – focus on factual findings and legal conclusions
Relevance of the decision for future asylum appeals in the Tenth Circuit

outline.chapter_title: II. Factual Background and Immigration Proceedings
outline.description: A detailed factual narrative explains who the petitioners are, their political activity in Colombia, the events that led to threats and violence by a narco‑guerrilla leader known as “Don Rafa,” their interactions with Colombian authorities, their entry into the United States without inspection, and the subsequent removal proceedings.
subtopics: Petitioners’ family composition, citizenship, and party affiliation with the Colombian Liberal Party
Political canvassing during the 2022 presidential election
Threatening phone calls beginning May 2022 and escalation after a colleague’s kidnapping/murder
Jiménez’s role as a provisional lawyer/intern with the National Prosecutor’s Office
Property dispute involving “Don Rafa” – discovery of narco‑trafficking operations at client’s property
Specific incidents: brochure threat, gunpoint intimidation at factory, assault on factory employee, attempted abduction at school
(Un)successful attempts to obtain assistance from Colombian police officers
Decision to flee Colombia and arrival in the United States in December 2022
Issuance of individual Notices to Appear (NTAs) and filing of asylum/withholding applications
Immigration judge’s denial reasoning – lack of past persecution, nexus, internal relocation feasibility, government protection
Board of Immigration Appeals affirmation

outline.chapter_title: III. Legal Framework Governing Asylum, Withholding of Removal, and Review Standards
outline.description: This chapter lays out the statutory definitions and elements for asylum under INA §1158(b), withholding under INA §1159(b), briefly notes CAT requirements (even though not appealed), allocates burdens of proof, explains evidentiary standards—preponderance for asylum claims versus substantial‑evidence review of BIA fact‑findings—and cites controlling precedent cited by the court.
subtopics: "Refugee" definition under INA §1101(a)(42)(A) – protected grounds (race, religion, nationality, particular social group, political opinion)
"Asylum" as discretionary relief – applicant bears burden by preponderance of evidence (8 U.S.C. §1158(b)(1))
"Withholding of removal" – higher burden requiring proven past persecution (see Niang v. Gonzales)
"Convention Against Torture" claim – elements (not reviewed)
"Past persecution" element – incident(s) constituting persecution plus nexus requirement
"Nexus" requirement – political opinion must be a central reason for harm
"Unable or unwilling" government protection analysis – reporting requirement & systemic inability
"Internal relocation" doctrine – safe‑relocation pre‑condition per 8 C.F.R. §1208.13(b)(1)(i)
"Standard of review" – substantial‑evidence for factual findings (Rivera‑Barrientos), de novo for legal conclusions (Singh v. Bondi)
"Scope of appellate review" under §1252(b)(4)(A) – reliance on administrative record

outline.chapter_title: IV. Determining Whether Past Persecution Occurred
outline.,description: The court’s application of Tenth Circuit precedent on what constitutes persecution is explored here—including why mere threats or psychological distress were found insufficient—and how each alleged incident was evaluated both individually and cumulatively.
subtopics: "Persecution" defined by case law – must involve serious harm beyond restrictions or sporadic threats (Wiransane v. Ashcroft; Karki v. Holder)
"Cumulative impact" test – assessing aggregate effect of multiple threats/assaults (Ritonga v. Holder)
Reviewing petitioners’ specific incidents: brochure threat (“death to snitches”), gunpoint intimidation at factory, assault on employee seeking petitioner whereabouts
Analysis of psychological/emotional harm claims — why courts have been reluctant to treat them alone as persecution (Brandy v. Holder)
"Substantial‑evidence" assessment – how record supported BIA finding that harms did not reach required level
"Implication for withholding" – failure to establish past persecution automatically defeats withholding claim

outline..chapter_title: V. Nexus Requirement: Political Opinion versus Personal Motive
outline..description: This chapter dissects the central‑reason test for political‑opinion nexus—examining whether petitioners proved that their Liberal Party affiliation was a primary cause of the hostility—while also noting their failure to articulate a particular social group argument.
.subtopics: "Central reason" standard – political opinion must be at least one primary motive for persecutor's conduct (Rivera‑Barrientos; Dallakoti v. Holder)
"Mixed‑motive analysis" – permissibility when persecutor has multiple reasons so long as protected ground is central
"Evidence presented": timing of escalated threats after Jiménez’s property dispute with Don Rafa;
"Court’s inference": threat motive rooted in Jiménez interfering with Don Rafa’s revenue rather than party activity;
"Absence*of particular social group argument*": why lack thereof weakens nexus claim;
"Precedent comparison*: Yuk v. Ashcroft — appellate courts do not re‑weigh evidence but assess whether substantial evidence supports lower tribunal

outline..chapter_title: VI. Government Protection / Internal Relocation Analysis and Final Holding
outline..description: The final analytical chapter addresses petitioner’s arguments that Colombia is unable or unwilling to protect them and that internal relocation is unsafe; it explains how the court applied reporting requirements and systemic‑government‑failure standards before concluding that petitioners failed both elements—and therefore were denied asylum and withholding.
.subtopics: "Unable or unwilling" framework – importance of applicant reporting abuse to authorities (Singh; Aviles‑Gonzalez)
"Petitioner's police interactions": single officer statements versus systemic government response;
"Government's actual conduct": searches/seizures at Don Rafa’s property indicating agency action against criminal activity;
"Futility exception": when reporting would be dangerous—why court found no sufficient proof thereof;

"Internal relocation feasibility": assessment under 8 C.F.R.… — family presence in countryside version;
            "Safe relocation demonstrated by three‑week stay outside Bogotá;
"Effect on withholding claim*": because asylum failed on core elements , withholding necessarily fails;

"Holding*: Denial of petition for review—affirmation of IJ/BIA decisions;
            "Policy implication*: reiterates high threshold for establishing persecution/nexus/government protection
